acadia.summary: Acadia National Park covers Mount Desert Island and several nearby islands along the Maine coast, where granite headlands meet the Atlantic. A loop road links shoreline, ponds and mountain summits, and a network of carriage roads crosses the interior. Fishing villages and harbor towns sit at the edges of the park.
acadia.whyGo: Come for a coastline of granite and spruce, a paved road that climbs to a summit above the sea, and carriage roads built for walking and cycling.

dayPlan.morning: Start on the Park Loop Road before the traffic builds and stop at Sand Beach and Thunder Hole. Walk a section of the Ocean Path where the surf hits the granite.
dayPlan.afternoon: Circle Jordan Pond and look up at the Bubbles, then pick a stretch of carriage road for a walk or ride under the trees. The gravel surface is wide and easy to follow.
dayPlan.evening: Drive to the quiet side of the island and stand below Bass Harbor Head Light as the light drops. Return along the shore road with the water still visible between the trees.

acadia.seasonNote: Summer and early fall bring the warmest weather and the fullest services. Cadillac Mountain summit access needs a vehicle reservation in season, and some park roads close in winter.
acadia.tip: Parking at the popular trailheads fills early. Pick one anchor for the morning and treat the rest of the day as flexible.

arches.summary: Arches National Park in eastern Utah holds more than two thousand documented stone arches along with fins, towers and balanced rocks. A scenic road climbs from the Colorado River into the formations, and trails range from short walks to longer desert routes. The rock is Entrada and Navajo sandstone, shaped by erosion over a long span of time.
arches.whyGo: Come to see a concentration of natural stone arches that is hard to match anywhere else, and to walk among fins and towers that change color through the day.

dayPlan.morning: Drive to Devils Garden and walk to Landscape Arch while the air is still cool. The path is mostly level and passes a series of smaller arches along the way.
dayPlan.afternoon: Move to The Windows and follow the short loops past North and South Window and Turret Arch. Take shade and water between stops rather than pushing through the heat.
dayPlan.evening: Walk to Delicate Arch for the last light, allowing enough time for the climb and the return. Bring a headlamp so the walk back does not depend on fading daylight.

arches.seasonNote: Spring and fall bring milder temperatures and the easiest walking. Summer heat is severe, and timed entry reservations apply during the busy season.
arches.tip: The Delicate Arch trail is exposed almost the whole way. Start it late enough for good light but carry enough water for the return in the dark.

badlands.summary: Badlands National Park in southwestern South Dakota spreads across eroded prairie, where layered rock walls and spires rise from grass. Bison, bighorn sheep and prairie dogs live on the mixed-grass prairie, and a loop road crosses the formations with frequent overlooks. The park is a mix of bare rock and open grassland rather than a single landscape.
badlands.whyGo: Come for the contrast between striped rock walls and open prairie, and for the chance to see bison and bighorn sheep without leaving the road for long.

dayPlan.morning: Drive the loop road and stop at the overlooks while the rock layers are still in low light. Walk the Door Trail boardwalk out onto the formations for a wider view.
dayPlan.afternoon: Take the Notch Trail if you are comfortable with a ladder and a narrow ledge, or choose a shorter prairie path instead. Watch the grassland for bison and give them room.
dayPlan.evening: Settle at an overlook near a prairie dog town as the light softens, then stay for sunset over the walls. The road is open late, so the drive back is easy.

badlands.seasonNote: Spring and fall bring milder temperatures. Summer afternoons are hot and exposed, and winter can close roads and leave ice on the trails.
badlands.tip: Bison are wild and fast. Stay in the vehicle or keep a wide distance on foot, and never approach an animal for a photograph.

big-bend.summary: Big Bend National Park in west Texas covers desert, river and mountain country along the Rio Grande. The Chisos Mountains rise from the desert floor, and canyons cut through limestone at the river's edge. It is a large, remote park with long drives between one place and the next.
big-bend.whyGo: Come for a scale of country that asks for time, with mountain trails, river canyons and desert road miles in the same park.

dayPlan.morning: Climb into the Chisos and walk the Lost Mine Trail for a view across the desert floor. Start early, because the trail is exposed on the upper sections.
dayPlan.afternoon: Drive to Santa Elena Canyon and walk the short path to where the river enters the rock walls. The canyon shade is welcome after the open road.
dayPlan.evening: Return to the Chisos Basin for sunset and a meal, then watch the sky darken over the peaks. The drive out is long, so plan it before you are tired.

big-bend.seasonNote: Spring and fall are the mildest seasons. Summer heat is intense in the desert, and the park is far from services, so carry water and plan fuel stops.
big-bend.tip: Cell service is limited and distances are long. Tell someone your route and keep a full water container in the vehicle.

biscayne.summary: Biscayne National Park protects Biscayne Bay and its islands south of Miami, with most of the park under water. Coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangrove shorelines support fish, manatees and birds. Access is mainly by boat, and the visitor center sits on the mainland shore.
biscayne.whyGo: Come for warm shallow water, a reef close to shore, and islands that feel far from the city even though the skyline is visible across the bay.

dayPlan.morning: Take a boat from the visitor center area and cross the bay while the water is calm. Choose a snorkel trip or a landing on one of the keys depending on conditions.
dayPlan.afternoon: Swim, snorkel or walk the shoreline, and give yourself time to dry off before the return crossing. Bring sun protection, since shade is limited on the water.
dayPlan.evening: Return across the bay as the light drops and the city appears in the distance. If you are camping, settle in before dark and secure food from birds and raccoons.

biscayne.seasonNote: Winter and spring bring clearer water and milder weather. Summer brings heat, storms and the chance of hurricanes, so check forecasts before booking a boat.
biscayne.tip: There is no bridge to the islands. Plan your visit around a concession boat, a private vessel or a guided tour, and reserve ahead in season.

black-canyon-of-the-gunnison.summary: Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park in western Colorado protects a steep, narrow canyon cut by the Gunnison River. Rock walls rise sharply from the water, and rim roads and overlooks look down into the gorge. The inner canyon is difficult country, and most visitors stay on the rim.
black-canyon-of-the-gunnison.whyGo: Come for a canyon that feels close and vertical, with overlooks that put the river far below and rock walls in shadow for much of the day.

dayPlan.morning: Stop at Gunnison Point and then drive the South Rim Road, taking the short walks to the overlooks. Morning light reaches different walls than it does later in the day.
dayPlan.afternoon: Walk a rim trail for a longer view, or drive to the North Rim if the road is open. The two sides look at each other across the gorge rather than at the same scene.
dayPlan.evening: Return to a west-facing overlook for sunset, when the rock turns warm and the river below goes dark. Keep back from the edge, since the drops are sudden.

black-canyon-of-the-gunnison.seasonNote: Late spring through early fall keeps the rim roads open. Winter closes the North Rim road and leaves the South Rim to snow and quiet.
black-canyon-of-the-gunnison.tip: The inner canyon routes are steep and unmarked in places. Treat them as serious undertakings and ask a ranger before starting one.

bryce-canyon.summary: Bryce Canyon National Park in southern Utah protects a series of natural amphitheaters filled with hoodoos, fins and spires of pink and orange rock. Rim trails look down into the formations, and trails descend among them. The park sits at high elevation, so nights are cool even in summer.
bryce-canyon.whyGo: Come to walk down among the hoodoos rather than only looking at them, and to see how the rock changes from the rim to the canyon floor.
highlights: Scenic drive to the high overlooks

dayPlan.morning: Start at Sunrise Point and descend the Queens Garden and Navajo Loop combination. The climb back out is steady, so take it slowly and let the morning cool work for you.
dayPlan.afternoon: Drive the scenic road south to the higher overlooks, stopping at Bryce Point and the quieter pullouts. The amphitheaters look different from each elevation.
dayPlan.evening: Walk a stretch of the rim trail as the light drops and the hoodoos cast long shadows. Stay for the stars, since the elevation and distance from cities keep the sky dark.

bryce-canyon.seasonNote: Summer days are mild at this elevation, and afternoon storms are common. Winter brings snow and closed roads, though the rim remains open.
bryce-canyon.tip: The trail down is easier than the trail up. Turn around before you feel tired, and remember that the elevation makes the climb harder than the distance suggests.

canyonlands.summary: Canyonlands National Park in southeastern Utah is divided by the Colorado and Green rivers into several districts. Island in the Sky sits on a high mesa with wide views, The Needles has rock spires and trails, and The Maze is remote and hard to reach. Distances between districts are long.
canyonlands.whyGo: Come for huge views from a mesa top, then for the quieter trails and rock shapes in the Needles if you have another day.

dayPlan.morning: Reach Mesa Arch before sunrise and watch the light come under the arch and onto the canyon below. Continue to Grand View Point for the wide look over the river country.
dayPlan.afternoon: Drive the rim road and take the short walks to the overlooks, or head to the Needles district if you have planned the extra distance. Carry water and fuel.
dayPlan.evening: Return to the mesa for sunset and stay until the sky is fully dark. The road back is unlit, so drive with care for wildlife.

canyonlands.seasonNote: Spring and fall are the mildest seasons. Summer heat is severe on the mesa, and winter can bring ice and closed back roads.
canyonlands.tip: The districts are far apart and not connected inside the park. Choose one district for the day instead of trying to see two.

capitol-reef.summary: Capitol Reef National Park in south-central Utah protects the Waterpocket Fold, a long wrinkle in the earth's crust. A scenic road follows the fold past cliffs of cream and red rock, and trails lead to arches and narrow canyons. Orchards and a small historic district sit along the Fremont River.
capitol-reef.whyGo: Come for a long wall of tilted rock, short trails to arches, and a valley of orchards that gives the place an unexpected softness.

dayPlan.morning: Walk to Hickman Bridge while the canyon is still cool. The trail climbs gently and passes under the arch, with a side view of another bridge below.
dayPlan.afternoon: Drive the scenic road along the fold and stop where the cliffs open up. If you want a longer walk, take the trail toward Cassidy Arch and its view over the valley.
dayPlan.evening: Spend the last light in Fruita among the orchards and the old buildings. The fruit trees and the river make a quiet end to a day of bare rock.

capitol-reef.seasonNote: Spring and fall are the mildest months. Summer heat builds in the canyon, and winter can bring snow and ice to the trails.
capitol-reef.tip: The park is long and narrow. Fill the fuel tank before you enter, since services inside are limited and the nearest town is some distance away.

carlsbad-caverns.summary: Carlsbad Caverns National Park in southeastern New Mexico protects a limestone cave system beneath the Chihuahuan Desert. The Big Room is a large chamber reached by elevator or by walking down through the Natural Entrance. Above ground, a desert drive and trails cross the mesa.
carlsbad-caverns.whyGo: Come to go underground into a huge decorated chamber, then to see how the desert above and the cave below belong to the same place.

dayPlan.morning: Walk down through the Natural Entrance if you are comfortable on a steep paved path, then tour the Big Room. The cave stays cool, so bring a layer.
dayPlan.afternoon: Take the desert drive or a short surface trail to see the country above the cave. The contrast with the underground rooms is part of the visit.
dayPlan.evening: Attend the bat flight in season if it is running, and watch from the amphitheater as the bats leave the cave. Keep voices low and put phones away.

carlsbad-caverns.seasonNote: The cave stays cool year round, and summer is the busiest season. Bat flights run in the warmer months, and elevator service can be limited.
carlsbad-caverns.tip: Reserve a cave entry time if the park requires one during your visit, and check the elevator status before you count on it.

channel-islands.summary: Channel Islands National Park protects five islands off the Southern California coast and the water around them. Each island has its own character, from sea cliffs and sea caves to grassland and scrub. Access is by boat or plane, and the islands grow quiet once the day visitors leave.
channel-islands.whyGo: Come for sea caves, clear water and island quiet, and for the crossing itself, where whales and dolphins sometimes appear.

dayPlan.morning: Take an early boat to Santa Cruz or Anacapa and use the crossing to watch for marine life. Land with a plan, since services on the islands are minimal.
dayPlan.afternoon: Hike an island trail or join a kayak trip into the sea caves if conditions allow. The water can be cold, so check what gear is provided.
dayPlan.evening: Return on the afternoon boat, or settle into a campground if you have a permit. The island feels different once the day boat has gone.

channel-islands.seasonNote: Summer and early fall bring the calmest crossings. Winter can be windy and rough, and boat schedules change with the season.
channel-islands.tip: Book the boat before you plan anything else. The crossing is the constraint, and the islands have no food or water for sale.
